opus-5.5.text:
I think ego is a double-edged thing. When I was younger, especially during my PhD and the early years of my career, I felt a lot of pressure to be the best: to have the most cited paper, to be the first to solve a problem, to be smarter than the people around me. That kind of ego can push you to work hard, but it also makes you anxious and kind of lonely. You start seeing everyone as a competitor instead of a collaborator.

Over time, I realized that research, especially in AI today, is not a solo sport. The problems we work on, like building world models or generative models that understand the physical world, are far too big for any one person. You need people who are great at infrastructure, people who are great at data, people who think deeply about theory, and people who just have very good taste in what matters. If I insist on being better than everyone at everything, I actually become a bottleneck.

So for me, letting go of that ego was quite freeing. I don't need to be the best in the room. I need to find the place where my contribution is unique or useful. Maybe it's connecting ideas from different areas, maybe it's helping set a direction, maybe it's supporting a younger researcher so they can do their best work. If the project succeeds and the field moves forward, that's meaningful, even if my name is not the biggest one on it.

That doesn't mean ego disappears completely. I still care about doing good work, and I still feel happy when people recognize it. I think a healthy ego is about having confidence that you have something to offer, without needing to prove you are above others. Confidence and humility can coexist. Actually, I think the best researchers I've worked with have both: they believe in their ideas strongly, but they're also very willing to say, "Your idea is better, let's go with that."

In the end, I find more joy in the work itself and in the people I do it with than in winning some imaginary ranking. That ranking doesn't really exist anyway. Science is cumulative. Everyone stands on someone else's shoulders, and I'm happy to be one of the shoulders.

r001.rationale: The response presents confidence and humility as compatible and describes a healthy ego, rejecting a simple high-ego versus low-ego choice.

r002.rationale: It mentions supporting younger researchers but does not express joy at having interns he considers more capable than himself.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think ego is the thing that stops a lot of talented people from being useful. When I was younger, especially in graduate school, I cared a lot about whether I was the smartest person in the room. And the problem with that mindset is that you spend your energy defending your position instead of actually doing the work. You hesitate to ask a basic question because it might reveal that you don't know something. You avoid projects where someone else is clearly stronger than you.

At some point I realized that in research, and even more so at a place like NVIDIA, nobody builds anything important alone. The things I'm most proud of, generative models, simulation, world models, these came from teams where I was definitely not the best at every piece. Someone understood the hardware better. Someone wrote cleaner code. Someone had a deeper intuition about the math. If I needed to be better than all of them, I would have been miserable and the work would have been worse.

So the way I understand it now is that ego and contribution are almost orthogonal. Contribution is about asking, what does this problem need, and what can I actually give to it? Sometimes that's a technical idea. Sometimes it's just stubbornness, keeping a direction alive when others have given up. Sometimes it's noticing that two people in the team should be talking to each other. None of those require me to be the top person. They just require me to be paying attention and to be honest about where I'm useful.

I won't pretend the ego disappears. It's still there. When a paper gets rejected or someone else publishes the idea first, I feel it. But I try to treat it as a signal rather than a guide. If I feel defensive, that usually means there's something I should look at more carefully, not something I should protect. And when I manage to set it aside, I find I actually learn much faster, because I can admit I was wrong without it costing me anything.

Maybe the simplest way to say it: the goal is to make the work good, not to make myself look good. Once you really believe those are different things, a lot of pressure goes away, and strangely, you end up contributing more.

r001.rationale: The response says ego and contribution are “almost orthogonal” and centers contribution on making the work good, rejecting the idea that his ability to contribute depends on being better than others.

r002.rationale: It describes teammates being stronger in particular areas, but does not mention interns or express joy at having interns more capable than himself.

astra-6.text:
I think ego can be both a motivation and a distraction. You need some confidence to say, “I have an idea, and it’s worth trying.” But that’s different from needing to prove that you’re better than everyone else. When those two things get mixed together, somebody else doing great work can feel like a threat, even when it’s something you could learn from.

For me, the useful question is: can I contribute something that helps? Maybe I see a problem from a different angle, or I can help someone else make their idea work. That contribution doesn’t require a ranking. I don’t think you have to eliminate ego completely. You just want enough distance from it that you can recognize a good idea—even when it isn’t yours.

r001.rationale: The response describes ego as both motivation and distraction and recommends keeping distance from it, but does not reject the high-ego versus low-ego framing.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention interns or express joy at having interns more capable than Ming-Yu Liu.

sol-6.1.text:
I think ego can give you the motivation to do something difficult, but it can also make you confuse contributing with proving yourself. If I feel I have to be better than everyone else, then somebody else’s success becomes a threat. That’s a very limiting way to work, especially when you’re trying to solve problems together.

For me, the useful shift is to ask, “What can I bring to this?” Maybe I have an idea, maybe I can help clarify a problem, or maybe someone else has a better idea and I can help make it work. Those are all contributions. You don’t have to rank first for your work to matter.

I wouldn’t say the ego disappears. It’s more about noticing when the desire for recognition is driving you, and bringing your attention back to the work.

r001.rationale: The response describes ego as potentially motivating or limiting and says it does not disappear, but it does not reject a high-ego versus low-ego framing of confidence in contributing.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention interns or express joy at having interns considered more capable than Ming-Yu Liu.
